start:
Red Cross Wilderness First Aid — Initial Triage:
Always assess scene safety before approaching. Use the ABC method: Airway, Breathing, Circulation. Identify the most life-threatening issue first. Do not move an injured person unless they are in immediate danger.
injury_assessment:
TCCC (Tactical Combat Casualty Care) — Hemorrhage Control Priority:
Severe bleeding is the leading preventable cause of death in wilderness emergencies. Address life-threatening bleeding before anything else. Apply tourniquet or direct pressure within the first 3 minutes for best outcomes.
bleeding_protocol:
TCCC — Hemorrhage Control:
For extremity wounds: tourniquet 2-3 inches above the wound, tighten until bleeding stops, note the time (safe for 2 hours). For junctional wounds (groin, armpit): wound packing with gauze, apply firm sustained pressure for 3 minutes. Do not remove packing once applied. Keep the patient warm — hypothermia worsens bleeding.
apply_tourniquet:
TCCC — Tourniquet Application:
Material must be at least 1.5 inches wide. Place tourniquet on bare skin when possible. Tighten windlass until radial pulse disappears distal to wound and bleeding stops. Mark time of application. A properly applied tourniquet is painful — this is expected and normal. Do not remove in the field.
pressure_dressing:
Red Cross — Wound Packing:
Pack wound firmly with the cleanest material available. Use a cloth strip, bandage, or clothing cut to approximately 2-inch width. Maintain steady pressure for at least 3 minutes without lifting. If blood soaks through, add more material on top — do not remove original packing.
lost_protocol:
NASAR (National Association for Search and Rescue) — Lost Person Protocol:
STOP: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan. Your last known position is where rescuers will begin searching. Moving makes you exponentially harder to find. Signal every 15-30 minutes using the rule of three (3 blasts, 3 fires, 3 flashes). Conserve energy and maintain body temperature.
signaling_protocol:
NASAR — Signaling Techniques:
Rule of Three: Any signal repeated 3 times is a universal distress signal. Whistle: 3 blasts = help needed. Mirror/reflector: aim at aircraft using hole-sighting method, visible up to 10 miles on clear days. Signal fire: build in clearing, 3 fires in triangle formation, add green leaves/rubber for smoke. Ground-to-air signals: X = need medical help, V = need help, arrow = direction traveling. Make signals large (min 10 feet).
signal_whistle:
NASAR — Whistle Signaling:
3 short blasts, pause 1 minute, repeat. A referee whistle can be heard up to 1 mile. Sound travels farther at dawn and dusk. Listen between blasts for response. If you hear responders, signal continuously to guide them to you.
signal_mirror:
NASAR — Mirror/Reflective Signaling:
Hold mirror 1 inch from face. Look through hole at target. Move mirror to align bright spot with target. Aircraft can detect mirror flash from 50+ miles in clear conditions. Use any reflective surface: phone screen, foil, watches. Signal in slow sweeping motion, not rapid flashing.
signal_fire:
NASAR — Fire Signaling:
Build fire in largest open area available — clearing, hilltop, or open ridgeline. Avoid building under tree canopy (blocks visibility). Three fires in a triangle (60-90 feet apart) is the international distress signal. For smoke (daytime): add green leaves, wet wood, rubber, plastic for black smoke (visible against sky). For night visibility: dry wood for bright flames.
signal_none:
NASAR — No Equipment Signaling:
Ground-to-air signals using rocks, logs, or clothing: X pattern minimum 10 feet across. Tramp a large arrow in snow showing direction of travel. Stomp SOS pattern in sand or snow (large, visible from aircraft). Bright clothing spread on open rock or clearing. Move to highest visible open ground without compromising shelter.
signal_ground_to_air:
NASAR — Stay Put Protocol:
Statistics show 97% of lost persons found within 3 miles of their last known position. Rescuers search outward from last known point. Movement creates multiple potential positions and complicates search. Only move if: in immediate life-threatening danger from weather/hazard, you can see definitive civilization, you have GPS and know the distance.
rescue_call:
NASAR — Emergency Communication Script:
State clearly: 1) Your name, 2) Your location (GPS coordinates or landmarks), 3) Number of people, 4) Nature of emergency, 5) Any injuries, 6) Your resources. Speak slowly — emergency operators are writing this down. Use phonetic alphabet for coordinates. Keep the line open if possible.
triage_selection:
Red Cross Wilderness First Aid — Secondary Survey:
After controlling life threats, systematically assess from head to toe. Look for: deformities, open wounds, tenderness, swelling. Ask about: mechanism of injury, symptoms, allergies, medications, last meal, events leading to injury.
splint_protocol:
Red Cross — Fracture Immobilization:
Immobilize the joint above and below the fracture. Pad all rigid materials to prevent pressure sores. Check circulation, sensation, and movement (CSM) before and after splinting. Fingers/toes should remain exposed to monitor color. Do not straighten angulated fractures — immobilize as found. Elevation reduces swelling.
anaphylaxis_protocol:
Red Cross — Anaphylaxis Recognition:
Signs: skin hives/flushing, swelling of face/lips/tongue/throat, difficulty breathing, wheezing, drop in blood pressure, rapid pulse, nausea/vomiting, dizziness. Onset typically within minutes of exposure. Anaphylaxis is a rapidly progressing, life-threatening emergency.
administer_epipen:
Red Cross — Epinephrine Auto-Injector:
Remove safety cap. Place against outer thigh (can inject through clothing). Press firmly until click — hold for 10 seconds. Remove and massage area for 10 seconds. Note exact time administered. Second dose can be given after 5-15 minutes if symptoms return. Position patient sitting upright if breathing difficulty, lying flat if dizzy/faint.
snake_bite_protocol:
CDC — Snakebite Field Management:
Immobilize the bitten limb at or below heart level. Remove jewelry/tight clothing near bite. Mark the edge of swelling with pen and time every 15 minutes. Keep patient calm and still — activity spreads venom faster. Do not: cut the wound, apply tourniquet, use suction device, apply ice, give alcohol. The ONLY treatment is antivenom at a hospital.
heat_protocol:
CDC — Heat Emergency Recognition:
Heat Exhaustion (milder): heavy sweating, pale/cool/moist skin, fast/weak pulse, nausea, muscle cramps, weakness, headache, fainting. Core temp usually below 104°F (40°C). Heat Stroke (severe emergency): no sweating or minimal, hot/red/dry skin, rapid/strong pulse, confusion, loss of consciousness. Core temp above 104°F (40°C). Heat stroke has 80% mortality if untreated.
heat_stroke:
CDC — Heat Stroke Treatment:
Rapid cooling is the only treatment that saves lives. Every minute counts. Best methods in order: cold water immersion (most effective), spray with cool water + fan, apply ice packs to neck/armpits/groin. Remove all clothing. Do not give fluids to unconscious patient. Keep cooling until patient becomes alert and oriented.
heat_exhaustion:
CDC — Heat Exhaustion Treatment:
Move to cool/shaded area. Remove excess clothing. Apply cool wet cloths to skin. Have patient slowly drink cool water if conscious (0.5-1L over 1 hour). Elevate legs. Monitor for progression to heat stroke (confusion, stops sweating, worsening condition) — if progression occurs, treat as heat stroke immediately.
hypothermia_protocol:
FEMA — Hypothermia Recognition:
Mild (32-35°C/90-95°F): shivering, clumsiness, slurred speech, poor judgment. Moderate (28-32°C/82-90°F): shivering stops (danger sign), muscle stiffness, slow/shallow breathing, confusion. Severe (<28°C/<82°F): unconscious, very weak pulse, barely breathing. Handle severe hypothermia extremely gently — cardiac arrest risk from rough movement.
active_rewarming:
FEMA/Wilderness Medicine — Rewarming Protocol:
Move to shelter immediately. Insulate from ground (ground draws heat 25x faster than air). Replace all wet clothing with dry. Apply heat to core areas (torso, armpits, groin, neck) not extremities. Use body-to-body contact for severe cases. Warm sweet drinks if patient is conscious and able to swallow. Do not rub extremities — drives cold blood to core. Gentle handling only for moderate/severe hypothermia.
concussion_protocol:
Red Cross WFA — Head Injury Assessment:
Ask: What happened? What year is it? Where are you? Confused/incorrect answers suggest significant brain injury. Monitor for: deteriorating consciousness, worsening headache, repeated vomiting (>2 times), seizures, clear fluid from nose/ears (CSF leak), unequal pupils. Any worsening is a medical emergency requiring immediate evacuation.
spinal_protocol:
Red Cross WFA — Spinal Precautions:
Spinal injury mechanism: fall from height, diving injury, high-speed collision, direct blow to spine. Do not move unless: life-threatening hazard, need to open airway (carefully), unconscious with no pulse (CPR takes priority). Use in-line manual stabilization if movement is absolutely necessary. Tell patient: Do not move your head. We are going to keep you still.
burn_protocol:
WHO — Burn Classification:
1st degree (superficial): red, dry, painful — no blisters. 2nd degree (partial thickness): blisters, moist, very painful. 3rd degree (full thickness): white/brown/black, leathery, painless (nerve damage). Critical burns requiring immediate evacuation: >10% body surface area, face/hands/feet/genitals/joints, circumferential burns, inhalation injury.
water_purification_info:
CDC — Water Safety:
All surface water in wilderness should be treated. Risk factors: animal waste, agricultural runoff, human activity upstream. Treatment methods by effectiveness: 1) Boiling (1 minute, 3 min at altitude >6500ft) — kills everything. 2) Chemical treatment (iodine, chlorine) — effective against bacteria/viruses, NOT cryptosporidium. 3) Filter (0.2 micron) — removes protozoa/bacteria, NOT viruses. 4) UV purification — kills all microorganisms. Best: filter + chemical treatment together.
shelter_protocol:
FEMA Wilderness Survival — Shelter Priority:
Exposure kills faster than dehydration or starvation. Shelter is priority #1 in cold/wet/windy conditions. Choose site: near water but not in flood zone, sheltered from prevailing wind, visible from air. Insulation principle: dead air space is what keeps you warm — use leaves, pine needles, grass to stuff into clothing and build bedding. Minimum 4 inches of insulation under body (ground contact kills).
disaster_selection:
FEMA / Red Cross — Natural Disaster Triage:
During any natural disaster, your priority is physical safety and following official evacuation orders. If you are in a safe location, stay put and monitor emergency broadcasts. Check yourself and others for injuries once the immediate threat has passed.
earthquake_protocol:
FEMA — Earthquake Safety (Drop, Cover, Hold On):
1) DROP: Get down on your hands and knees. This protects you from falling and keeps you low to the ground. 2) COVER: Protect your head and neck with your arms. If possible, crawl under a sturdy table or desk. 3) HOLD ON: Stay in place until the shaking stops. If outdoors, move away from buildings, streetlights, and utility wires. If in a vehicle, pull over to a clear location.
earthquake_aftermath:
FEMA — Earthquake Post-Shaking Safety:
Expect aftershocks, which can happen minutes, hours, or days after the main event. Check for structural damage and gas leaks. If you smell gas or hear a hissing sound, open a window and leave immediately. Do not use matches, lighters, or any electrical switches until you are sure there are no gas leaks. Stay out of damaged buildings.
flood_protocol:
Red Cross — Flood Safety (Turn Around, Don't Drown):
Never walk, swim, or drive through floodwaters. 6 inches of fast-moving water can knock you over; 12 inches can carry away most cars. If you are caught on a flooded road and your car stalls, leave it and move to higher ground immediately. Do not climb into an attic unless you have a way to get onto the roof (e.g., an axe).
flood_safety:
Red Cross — Flood Health & Hazard Safety:
Stay away from power lines and electrical equipment — electrocution is a major risk in floods. Avoid contact with floodwater, which may be contaminated with sewage, chemicals, or sharp debris. Do not eat food or drink water that has touched floodwater. Monitor local authorities for water safety alerts (Boil Water Advisories).
wildfire_protocol:
Red Cross — Wildfire Safety & Evacuation:
If told to evacuate, do so immediately. Close all windows and doors to reduce drafts. Shut off gas at the meter if time permits. If trapped indoors: stay inside, move away from windows, and keep everyone together in the center of the building. Fill sinks and tubs with water for emergency use. Outside: find an area clear of vegetation, or a body of water if possible.
storm_protocol:
FEMA — Tornado and Severe Storm Safety:
Go to a pre-designated safe room or basement. If no basement is available, go to an interior room on the lowest floor (like a bathroom or closet) away from windows. Protect your head and neck with your arms or a heavy blanket. If outdoors and unable to reach shelter, lie flat in a nearby ditch or depression and cover your head.
poisoning_protocol:
CDC / American Association of Poison Control Centers — Poisoning Response:
1) Identify the substance and amount. 2) If swallowed: DO NOT induce vomiting or give anything by mouth unless instructed by a professional. 3) If on skin/eyes: Rinse with clean water for at least 15 minutes. 4) If inhaled: Move to fresh air immediately. 5) Call Poison Control or Emergency Services. Bring the container/sample with you if you evacuate.
skills_selection:
US Army Survival Manual (FM 21-76) — Basic Survival Skills:
Survival is a matter of mental attitude as much as physical skill. Prioritize your needs using the Rule of Threes: You can survive 3 minutes without air, 3 hours without shelter in extreme conditions, 3 days without water, and 3 weeks without food. Stay calm and follow these protocols.
water_skills:
SAS Survival Handbook — Water Procurement:
Water is your second priority after shelter. Never wait until you are out of water to look for more. Avoid drinking untreated water if possible, but dehydration kills faster than most water-borne pathogens. Conserve water by: staying in the shade, breathing through your nose, and not eating (digestion uses water).
solar_still_info:
US Army FM 21-76 — Belowground Solar Still:
1) Dig a hole 3ft wide by 2ft deep in a sunny spot (clay or damp soil is best). 2) Place a clean container in the center. 3) Line the pit with non-poisonous green vegetation (optional, adds moisture). 4) Cover the pit with a clear plastic sheet, sealing the edges with dirt to trap air. 5) Place a small rock in the center of the plastic directly over the container. 6) Solar heat evaporates moisture which condenses on the plastic and drips into the container. Yields 0.5 to 1 liter per day.
transpiration_info:
US Army FM 21-76 — Transpiration Bag:
1) Find a healthy, non-poisonous tree with green leaves. 2) Place a large, clear plastic bag over a branch. 3) Tie the bag tightly around the branch to ensure an airtight seal. 4) Ensure the bag is angled so that water will pool in a corner. 5) The tree's natural transpiration will produce condensation inside the bag. Yields about 0.2 to 0.5 liters per day. Do not use if the tree has milky sap.
finding_water_info:
SAS Survival Handbook — Natural Water Indicators:
1) Gravity: Water flows downhill; look in valley bottoms and gullies. 2) Vegetation: Lush green growth in an otherwise dry area indicates water near the surface. 3) Animals: Birds (especially pigeons/finches) fly toward water at dawn/dusk. Bees fly in a straight line toward water. Animal tracks often lead downhill to water sources. 4) Digging: In dry stream beds, dig at the outside of a bend or the lowest point — water may be just below the surface.
food_skills:
US Army FM 21-76 — Survival Food:
Food is your lowest priority in the short term. Do not eat if you are low on water, as digestion requires significant fluid. Prioritize insects (crickets, grasshoppers, ants) as they are high in protein and easy to catch. Avoid brightly colored insects or those with stings.
edibility_test:
SAS Survival Handbook — Universal Edibility Test:
1) Test only one part of one plant at a time. 2) Rub on skin (inner elbow) for 15 mins. If no reaction, continue. 3) Touch to outer lip for 3 mins. No reaction? 4) Place on tongue for 15 mins. Do not swallow. 5) Chew a small piece for 15 mins without swallowing. 6) If still no reaction, swallow and wait 8 hours. If sick, induce vomiting. If fine, eat a handful and wait another 8 hours. WARNING: Never test mushrooms or plants with milky sap.
safe_plants_info:
US Army FM 21-76 — Common Edible Plants:
1) Dandelions: All parts edible (leaves raw, roots roasted for 'coffee'). 2) Pine: Young needles make a tea high in Vitamin C (steep, do not boil). 3) Cattails: Roots are starchy and can be boiled/baked; young shoots taste like cucumber. 4) Grasses: Seeds of all grasses are edible (grind into flour), and the base of stalks is often tender and sweet.
avoid_plants_info:
US Army FM 21-76 — Plants to Avoid:
Avoid any plant with: 1) Milky or colored sap. 2) Red berries (unless known). 3) White or yellow berries (almost always poisonous). 4) Umbrella-shaped flower clusters (looks like wild carrot/parsnip — high risk of deadly Hemlock). 5) Three-leaf clusters (Poison Ivy/Oak). 6) Bitter or soapy taste. 7) Spines, fine hairs, or thorns (unless known).
shelter_skills:
US Army FM 21-76 — Shelter Principles:
Shelter protects you from wind, rain, and temperature extremes. Site selection: Avoid low ground (flash floods/cold air), dead trees (falling branches), and insect nests. Insulation is key — you lose more heat to the ground than the air. Always build a bed of at least 6 inches of dry debris (leaves, grass, pine needles).
snow_shelter:
SAS Survival Handbook — Snow Cave:
1) Find a deep snow drift at least 5ft deep. 2) Dig a tunnel into the side, then expand upward to create a chamber. 3) The floor of the chamber must be higher than the entrance tunnel (to trap rising warm air). 4) Poke a small ventilation hole through the roof with a stick. 5) Smooth the inside of the roof to prevent dripping. 6) Block the entrance with a block of snow or a pack, leaving a small air gap.
desert_shelter:
US Army FM 21-76 — Desert Survival Shelter:
1) Dig a trench 1.5ft deep and as long as your body. 2) Pile sand around the edges for extra depth. 3) Cover the trench with a double-layered roof (tarp, clothing, or branches) leaving a 4-inch gap between layers — this 'air gap' provides insulation against the sun's heat. 4) Digging down just a few inches can lower the temperature by 10-20 degrees. Stay in the shade and minimize activity during the heat of the day.
nav_skills:
US Army FM 21-76 — Primitive Navigation:
When you have no compass, use the environment. In the Northern Hemisphere, moss often grows more thickly on the north side of trees (less sun). Trees on south-facing slopes are often larger and more lush. Follow watercourses downhill; they eventually lead to larger rivers and human settlement.
shadow_tip_info:
US Army FM 21-76 — Shadow-Tip Method:
1) Place a straight stick vertically in the ground in a sunny spot. 2) Mark the very tip of the shadow with a stone or stick. 3) Wait 15-20 minutes until the shadow moves several inches. 4) Mark the new position of the shadow tip. 5) Draw a straight line between the two marks. This is your East-West line. 6) The first mark is always WEST, and the second is always EAST. A line perpendicular to this points North-South.
polaris_info:
NASA / US Army — Finding North (Northern Hemisphere):
1) Locate the Big Dipper (Ursa Major). 2) Find the two stars at the outer edge of the 'cup' (Dubhe and Merak). 3) Follow the line formed by these two stars outward from the cup for about five times the distance between them. 4) The bright star you reach is Polaris (the North Star). It is almost exactly over True North. The height of Polaris above the horizon is also roughly equal to your Latitude.
southern_cross_info:
SAS Survival Handbook — Finding South (Southern Hemisphere):
1) Locate the Southern Cross (Crux). 2) Find the two 'pointer stars' nearby (Alpha and Beta Centauri). 3) Extend the long axis of the cross downward. 4) Find the point where an imaginary line from between the pointer stars intersects the extended axis of the cross. 5) This point is the South Celestial Pole. Dropping a vertical line from this point to the horizon indicates True South.
